title: Axioms of probability and geometric probability

steps.title: Kolmogorov axioms
steps.idea: Throw darts at random into the unit square $\Omega$. An event is a region, and its probability is the share of darts it catches. Three rules are all that probability needs: it is never negative, the whole square has probability $1$, and for disjoint events the probabilities add.

layers.intuition: While the strips do not touch, every dart in $A \cup B$ is counted once on the left bar, so the two bars stand level. The white tick is the exact area.
layers.definition: A probability is a function $P$ on the events of $\Omega$ with $P(A) \ge 0$, $P(\Omega) = 1$, and $P\bigl(\bigcup_i A_i\bigr) = \sum_i P(A_i)$ for pairwise disjoint $A_1, A_2, \dots$
layers.details: Everything else follows: $P(\varnothing) = 0$, $P(\bar A) = 1 - P(A)$, $P(A) \le P(B)$ when $A \subset B$, and $P(A) \le 1$.

steps.title: When events overlap
steps.idea: Widen $B$ until it reaches into $A$. Now the darts in the overlap $AB$ are counted twice by $P(A) + P(B)$, and the left bar outgrows the right one by exactly that share. Subtract it and the sum is right again.

layers.definition: For any events $A$ and $B$: $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(AB)$. It follows from the axioms, since $A \cup B$ is the disjoint union of $A$ and $B \setminus A$.

steps.title: Probability is area
steps.idea: When a point is thrown at random into a region $\Omega$, the chance of landing in $A$ is the share of area that $A$ takes. Take the quarter disc in the unit square: its area is $\pi/4$, so four times the share of hits estimates $\pi$.

layers.definition: Geometric probability: if a point is thrown at random into a region $\Omega$ of finite measure, so that the chance of hitting a part depends only on its measure, then $P(A) = \operatorname{mes} A / \operatorname{mes} \Omega$.
layers.details: This is the Monte Carlo method in one picture. The error of $\hat\pi$ shrinks like $1/\sqrt{n}$: each new correct digit costs about a hundred times more darts.

steps.title: Buffon's needle
steps.idea: Drop a needle of length $l$ on a floor ruled with lines $d$ apart. Its centre and its angle are random, and it crosses a line with probability $2l/(\pi d)$. Count the crossings and $\pi$ appears from a floor and a needle.

layers.details: Let $x \in [0, d/2]$ be the distance from the centre to the nearer line and $\theta \in [0, \pi]$ the angle. The pair is uniform on a rectangle of area $\pi d/2$, and the needle crosses when $x \le \tfrac{l}{2}\sin\theta$. The area under that curve is $\int_0^\pi \tfrac{l}{2}\sin\theta\,d\theta = l$, so $P = \dfrac{l}{\pi d/2} = \dfrac{2l}{\pi d}$.

steps.title: Bertrand's paradox
steps.idea: What is the chance that a chord taken at random is longer than the side $\sqrt3$ of the inscribed triangle? Three natural ways to take a chord give three answers, $1/2$, $1/3$ and $1/4$. Each is right for its own experiment: "at random" means nothing until the law is named.

layers.intuition: A point on a radius at distance below $1/2$ from the centre gives a long chord: half of the radius. Two random ends make a long chord when the central angle is over $120°$: a third of the circle. A midpoint inside the circle of radius $1/2$: a quarter of the area.
